_note: Single source of truth for every number on the website and in marketing. Verified measurements only. Do not invent or round up.
name: Sparrow Decider
disclaimer: Unofficial community project. Not an AWS or Strands product.
license: Apache-2.0 (code); model weights derived from MIT-licensed potion-base-8M and Ettin encoders
what: Decision models that answer yes/no, pick-one and score questions about a state, with calibrated probabilities, in the same shapes as Strands Decider. From a 47 MB model on a laptop down to a ~2 KB compiled model on a microcontroller.

tiers.quality: general text decisions; JevBench 122/231, MASSIVE intent 0.588

headline_numbers.label: per text decision on the same chip (sparrow-nano-general)
navigation calls from sensor numbers right with a 1.11 MB nano-robot; the public 2-billion-parameter decider gets 3 / 10
Python install; C99 runtime with no malloc

board: ESP32-S3 (QFN56 rev0.2), 240 MHz, 16 MB flash, 8 MB PSRAM
runtimes: C99, no malloc, model read from flash (ESP-IDF component)
sparrow-pico compiler: device spec -> C header
how_it_works: A full Strands Decider (4B) teaches the text tiers through distillation on ~430k decisions.
nano: static embeddings, pruned 8-16k vocabulary, 128-d, plus key-value number pooling that reads 'battery: 6%' as a value.
pico: you write a spec (sensors, rules, questions); the public Strands Decider 2B labels sampled states; the compiler writes one tiny MLP per question as C.
On the ESP32-S3: int8 SIMD on the vector unit (ESP-NN kernel), weights in PSRAM / internal RAM.
honest_limits: Open-ended language it never trained on: well behind the 2B (MASSIVE domain routing 0.37-0.67 across released Sparrow models vs 0.86).
Yes/no judgement on JevBench is near chance at every tier.
pico answers only the questions it was compiled for.

pico.question: What should the robot do next?

parity: The C runtime matches the Python runtime to within 1e-5 on the host; on the ESP32-S3, int8 builds agree with the host on 150-155 of 155 decisions.
speedups_note: First on-chip build vs today, same board. Today's nano models also use a smaller hidden layer.
